title: Contract automation: Owning delivery enables embedded feedback
desc: Presents Crosby’s organizational model of legal expertise, ownership and entrepreneurial development rather than validated performance evidence.

kps.k: Crosby presents organisational design, not just software, as the route to contract automation.
kps.d: In the publisher’s transcript, the founders describe an AI-first law firm focused on contracts: delivering the work lets them understand lawyers’ workflows and attempt to replace as much as possible with agentic systems, aiming to close contracts faster. Their distinctive proposition combines legal-service delivery with product development rather than selling a standalone tool. They present negotiation automation as a theory; the supplied material does not establish achieved automation rates or faster closure.

qs.q: So the theory is that we can automate human negotiations, so getting people to agree on terms.
qs.a: Deal Velocity, Not Billable Hours: How Crosby Uses AI to Redefine Legal Contracting — publisher's transcript · AI-native providers · 2025

qs.q: And it turns out the best way to do this and to automate it is by building an in-house law firm, understanding how lawyers work and then trying to replace as much of that agentically to get contracts closed faster.
qs.a: Deal Velocity, Not Billable Hours: How Crosby Uses AI to Redefine Legal Contracting — publisher's transcript · AI-native providers · 2025

kps.k: Embedded legal expertise supplies the feedback that the proposed automation model depends on.
kps.d: The founders describe small teams combining experienced legal specialists, promising graduates and entrepreneurial engineers, with one or two lawyers working alongside engineers. They argue that proximity to the user accelerates development and product feedback, while autonomy gives engineers ownership of problems. This makes human expertise an input to automation rather than something the firm can simply dispense with. The accounts describe practices and expected benefits, not measured productivity gains or the extent of human verification still required.

qs.q: It’s such a unique opportunity in terms of the amount of dev cycles and product loops you get.
qs.a: Deal Velocity, Not Billable Hours: How Crosby Uses AI to Redefine Legal Contracting — publisher's transcript · AI-native providers · 2025

qs.q: But um but what's interesting is in this type of company which is in a lot of these on the application layer um as John mentioned you need that level of autonomy and agency and creativity of that fundamentality of like this is my thing and I'm going to figure out how to build it um with my pot of lawyers and I'm going to I'm going to solve this and  then I'm going to come back.
qs.a: Ryan Daniels & John Sarihan (Crosby) — Sequoia Training Data Ep.61 · AI-native providers · 2026

kps.k: Crosby recruits entrepreneurial talent by offering ownership and development, including preparation to leave and found a company.
kps.d: The founders describe employment as a four- or five-year stepping stone and say they must honour that promise, for example by sending employees to founder dinners. The Neofirm profile traces Sarihan’s emphasis on growth potential and speed to his Ramp experience and reports that he welcomes both long-term employees and future founders. The practical implication is a recruiting bargain built around development and access, not retention alone. The profile also portrays lawyers’ frustration with traditional-firm tedium as a motivation to join, without establishing how widespread that preference is.

qs.q: And the way that we’ve been able to convince people to join us is by saying, “This will be your stepping stone for four or five years.” And we have to live up to that, by the way.
qs.a: Deal Velocity, Not Billable Hours: How Crosby Uses AI to Redefine Legal Contracting — publisher's transcript · AI-native providers · 2025

qs.q: I want to hire people who are either like: this is my last job, or this is my second to last job because I’m starting a company after.
qs.a: Crosby: The Inner Workings of a Neofirm · Market & press · 2026

kps.k: Leadership and service culture feature as proposed enablers, but the evidence remains an organisational portrait.
kps.d: The Neofirm author, employees and investor Ryan Kim portray Ryan’s people-oriented leadership and Sarihan’s pragmatic execution as complementary. Anecdotes about task decomposition, candid feedback and impatience with delay illustrate the reported culture. The author interprets the ambition as a seamless end-to-end service, explicitly presenting that motivation as an impression. These accounts do not demonstrate that leadership style causes better legal outcomes. The supplied material contains no direct counterargument; its central unresolved question is whether the described culture translates into reliable, scalable service.

qs.q: If Ryan is philosophical, charismatic, a steward of people, John Sarihan, Crosby’s CTO, is a deeply pragmatic and an execution oriented thought partner.
qs.a: Crosby: The Inner Workings of a Neofirm · Market & press · 2026

qs.q: Ryan Kim, a partner at Bain Capital Ventures who incubated Crosby, shared with me one of Ryan’s essential skills is “sincerity” and intellectual curiosity, fantastic at “creating reality distortion fields,” while John is all “fast clock speeds and quiet competence.” The abrasion is good for them.
qs.a: Crosby: The Inner Workings of a Neofirm · Market & press · 2026

kps.k: The founders cast New York’s expertise, engineering talent and design culture as advantages, not demonstrated determinants of success.
kps.d: They associate New York with dense domain expertise, experienced engineers and design quality, contrasting it with San Francisco’s AI ideation culture. They also credit Ramp with encouraging future founders. Support consists chiefly of personal observations, career histories and an uncertain recollection of a survey about graduates’ 2021–2022 location preferences. They acknowledge uncertainty about what makes founder-oriented hiring specifically New York-based, and their expectation of another startup wave is prospective. Crosby’s craftsmanship-and-modernity naming story expresses this identity but remains an acknowledged myth, not evidence of a geographic advantage.

qs.q: What happened in the last five to ten years is, you know, more and more senior engineers were coming out of those places to the point where a lot of what building a startup is about is actually knowing what a great growth trajectory looks like and understanding how do you not just go from, like, one to ten but zero to one.
qs.a: Deal Velocity, Not Billable Hours: How Crosby Uses AI to Redefine Legal Contracting — publisher's transcript · AI-native providers · 2025

qs.q: I think one other uniquely New  York thing is just the emphasis it feels like on design.
qs.a: Ryan Daniels & John Sarihan (Crosby) — Sequoia Training Data Ep.61 · AI-native providers · 2026

vlens.an: The AI-native legal-provider voice supports the cluster’s principal proposition that Crosby treats ownership of legal-service delivery—not standalone software—as the organisational route to contract automation. Across the paired records, the founders argue that operating a law firm exposes lawyers’ workflows and enables attempts to automate parts of contract negotiation through agentic systems. They also consistently identify embedded lawyer–engineer–customer pods as the mechanism for rapid development and product-feedback loops, with entrepreneurial autonomy and founder-oriented career development supporting recruitment. Material variation is mainly one of emphasis: the publisher transcript foregrounds the automation thesis, while the Sequoia account gives greater weight to team design, talent development and New York’s founder and design culture. Those geographic claims are explicitly tentative and observational. Neither record supplies measured automation rates, faster-closing results, productivity gains, reliability evidence or the extent of human verification required. The records also substantially overlap in speakers and content, so they should be treated as closely related presentations of Crosby’s founder strategy rather than independent corroboration or evidence of wider agreement among AI-native legal providers.

qs.q: And it turns out the best way to do this and to automate it is by building an in-house law firm, understanding how lawyers work and then trying to replace as much of that agentically to get contracts closed faster.

qs.q: I think that mentality is really what it takes because in some ways like Ryan said, you're like building these pods and like these you're working with one or two lawyers and your customer is sitting right next to you is like such a unique opportunity in terms of like the amount of dev cycles and like product loops you get  and I think that's really special.
qs.a: Ryan Daniels & John Sarihan (Crosby) — Sequoia Training Data Ep.61 · AI-native providers · 2026

vlens.an: This press/profile source supports the proposition that Crosby’s distinctiveness lies in its organisational and service model, while stopping short of validating automation performance. It depicts the company as pursuing a seamless end-to-end legal service, supported by complementary leadership, execution-focused culture and a recruitment bargain aimed at both long-term employees and prospective founders. That aligns with the synthesis’s account of ownership, entrepreneurial development and service culture as proposed enablers. Material variation lies in the evidentiary basis: some claims come from employees and an investor, while the service ambition is explicitly the author’s impression. The source offers no measured evidence that this model produces faster contract closure, reliable automation, scalable delivery or reduced human verification, so its support is organisational and anecdotal rather than performance-based.

elens.an: The 2026 sources support the proposition that Crosby treats organisational design and ownership of legal-service delivery as the basis for embedded product feedback, rather than offering validated evidence of contract-automation performance. Across the sources, the common mechanism is close collaboration among engineers, lawyers and customers, reinforced by autonomy, speed, entrepreneurial hiring and an end-to-end service ambition. Material variation lies in emphasis and evidentiary basis: the founders describe team pods and rapid product loops directly, while the Neofirm profile concentrates on complementary leadership, execution culture and recruiting lawyers or future founders. Both are principally organisational accounts; neither establishes achieved automation rates, faster contract closure, scalable reliability or the extent of human verification required. The geographic claims about New York are especially tentative and impressionistic rather than demonstrated determinants of success.
